extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of political economy / political economy scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of classical political‑economy principles explaining (1) how man's propensity to exchange produces the division of labour and its limits, and (2) the origin, nature, and measures of money and price (value in use/exchange and labour as the real measure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Propensity to truck, barter, and exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: Man has a natural propensity to truck, barter, and exchange; when he needs the co-operation of others he will interest their self‑love rather than appeal to their benevolence. Offers and bargains (‘Give me that which I want, and you shall have this which you want’) are the ordinary means by which people obtain most of the good offices they require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by animal contrasts (puppy fawning, spaniel seeking food) and human behaviour: we address others' self‑interest not their humanity; only beggars chiefly depend on charity; most sustenance is obtained by treaty, barter, and purchase. Emphasises self‑interest as the driver of exchange rather than benevolence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labour arises from the power to exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: The disposition to truck, barter, and exchange originally gives occasion to the division of labour: individuals find it advantageous to specialise in occupations where they have dexterity and to exchange surplus for other goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in a tribe someone becomes an armourer (bows and arrows), another a house‑carpenter, another a smith, another a tanner. The certainty of being able to exchange surplus output encourages men to dedicate themselves to particular occupations and to bring talents to perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labour is limited by the extent of the market
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent of the division of labour is always limited by the extent of the market; where the market is very small there is little encouragement to specialise entirely in one employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples: a porter needs a large town; a village cannot support many specialised trades; country workmen must often perform many related branches (e.g., country carpenter = joiner, cabinet‑maker, carver, wheelwright). The principle explains why some industries exist only in large markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transport and market size determine industrial subdivision and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvements in means of transport (especially water‑carriage) open more extensive markets and thereby permit earlier and greater subdivision of industry; inland regions typically improve later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative contrast provided: broad‑wheeled waggons vs ships between London and Edinburgh (ship carries far more with far fewer men), showing how water‑carriage lowers transport costs and supports much more commerce. Historical/geographic examples: coastal Mediterranean, Nile canals in Egypt, rivers in Bengal and China, contrasted with inland Africa and Siberia where navigation is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference of talents often results from specialization (habit, custom, education)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent great differences in genius among professions (e.g., philosopher vs street porter) often arise less from nature and more from the effects of division of labour through habit, custom, and education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: children initially similar are put to different occupations early in life; the difference of talents widens by degrees as habit and training take effect. Thus the division of labour not only reflects differences but creates and magnifies them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of money: to overcome the inconveniences of barter
rubrics_metrics.description: When division of labour makes most goods be acquired by exchange, the double coincidence of wants frequently obstructs exchanges; people therefore naturally keep some commodity thought widely acceptable in exchange to facilitate trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples of common instruments of commerce: cattle, salt, certain shells, dried cod, tobacco, sugar, hides; practical explanation of why a commonly accepted medium eases transactions when direct barter fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metals preferred as instruments of commerce for practical reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Metals (particularly gold and silver) were ultimately preferred for use as money because they are durable (scarce perishable), divisible without loss (can be subdivided and reunited), and thus especially fit as instruments of commerce and circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes on earlier uses: iron among Spartans, copper among Romans; lists reasons why metals outperform cattle or other commodities in facilitating varied exchanges and allowing purchases of fractional values rather than whole animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coinage and public stamps to ensure uniform weight and fineness
rubrics_metrics.description: The trouble of weighing and assaying metal led to the institution of coined money with public stamps (mints) to ascertain quantity and uniform goodness; such stamped coins could be received by tale rather than by weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains assaying and weighing difficulties (especially with precious metals); analogises mints to aulnagers and stamp‑masters; cites early unstamped bars and the development of stamped coins (Servius Tullius in Rome) and the practical benefits of coinage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denominations originally expressed weight; debasement impacts creditors and debtors
rubrics_metrics.description: Coin denominations originally corresponded to specific weights/quantities of metal (e.g., Roman as, English pound sterling originally contained a pound of silver). Sovereigns who reduced the metal content debased coins, which favored debtors and defrauded creditors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical notes on Roman, English, French, and Scots pounds and pennies; observation that princes' debasements (reducing real metal content) let debtors pay nominal sums with less real value, producing harm to creditors and sometimes large private misfortunes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'value in use' and 'value in exchange'
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'value' has two meanings: 'value in use' (utility of an object) and 'value in exchange' (power of purchasing other goods). Things with greatest use (water) may have little exchange value; things with little use (diamond) may have great exchange value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets up the classical paradox of value and frames the investigation into what determines exchangeable value, preparing the later analysis of prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labour as the real measure of exchangeable value
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of any commodity to its possessor, insofar as he means to exchange it, equals the quantity of labour which it enables him to purchase or command; labour is the real measure of the exchangeable value of all commodities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims 'labour was the first price' — originally all wealth was purchased by labour rather than gold; the real price is the toil and trouble of acquiring something, and things bought with money/goods are equivalent to labour because they save toil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold method for analysing price (announced plan)
rubrics_metrics.description: To investigate exchangeable value the author will: (1) show the real measure of exchangeable value (real price); (2) show the different parts composing that real price; and (3) examine circumstances that sometimes raise or sink these parts above/below their natural rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit analytic rubric for the subsequent treatment of price: measure, components, and causes of deviation from natural price; reader advised patience for potentially tedious abstract exposition.
